title: Two Pointers
summary: Use two **pointers** with a clear movement rule.
refresher: **Two pointers** track two positions at the same time. The important part is the **movement rule**: each move should remove choices you no longer need.
refresher_code:
left = 0
right = len(nums) - 1
while left < right:
    total = nums[left] + nums[right]

advanced-tp-purpose.title: Two pointers avoid extra scanning
advanced-tp-purpose.body: **Two pointers** let you move from both ends or keep two related positions.
advanced-tp-purpose.example: left starts at 0, right starts at n - 1
advanced-tp-purpose.notice: The movement rule is the whole solution.
advanced-tp-purpose.mistake: Moving both **pointers** every time can skip valid answers.

advanced-tp-sorted-sum.title: Too small means move left
advanced-tp-sorted-sum.body: In a sorted **list**, moving left rightward gives a larger left **value**.
advanced-tp-sorted-sum.notice: Sorted order is what makes this safe.
advanced-tp-sorted-sum.mistake: Moving right when the sum is too small usually makes the sum even smaller.

advanced-tp-large-sum.title: Too large means move right
advanced-tp-large-sum.body: In a sorted **list**, moving right leftward gives a smaller right **value**.
advanced-tp-large-sum.notice: You are lowering the larger side of the pair.
advanced-tp-large-sum.mistake: Moving left when the sum is too large can make the sum larger.

advanced-tp-common-bug.title: Move with a reason
advanced-tp-common-bug.body: Every **pointer** move should come from the comparison you just made.
advanced-tp-common-bug.mistake: **Pointer** changes that are not tied to the **condition** often skip answers.

sections.title: What two pointers mean
sections.summary: Two positions work together to shrink the work.

blocks.body: A two-**pointer** solution keeps two **indexes** and moves one only when a comparison or rule says that side is done. The pointers might start at opposite ends, or one might follow behind the other.

blocks.title: Move one pointer for a reason
blocks.caption: Compare left and right in a sorted pair-sum search.

sections.title: Opposite-end pointers
sections.summary: Use both ends when sorted order or mirrored positions matter.

blocks.body: **Opposite-end pointers** start far apart and move inward. This shape fits sorted pair searches, palindrome checks, and problems where the outside values decide what can be ignored.

blocks.caption: The movement should match the evidence from the comparison.
blocks.wrong:
sum is too large
move left anyway
blocks.right:
sum is too large
move right leftward

blocks.prompt: In a sorted pair-sum search, why move right when the sum is too large?
choices: A smaller right value can lower the sum
It checks the same pair again
blocks.why: Sorted order makes the value at the new right position less than or equal to the old right value.

blocks.body: For sorted pair-sum problems, left points to a smaller **value** and right points to a larger value. If the sum is too small, left moves rightward to raise it. If the sum is too large, right moves leftward to lower it.

blocks.caption: Sorted two-sum moves one **pointer** based on the sum.

blocks.prompt: The sum is too large in a sorted **list**. Which **pointer** usually moves?
blocks.why: Moving right leftward chooses a smaller right **value**.

sections.title: Same-direction pointers
sections.summary: Sometimes one **pointer** reads while another writes or remembers a boundary.

blocks.body: Not every two-pointer problem starts at both ends. Some use a **read pointer** to scan each item and a **write pointer** to place kept values, remove duplicates, or compact a list.

blocks.caption: This pattern keeps values that should remain while `read` scans across the input.

blocks.prompt: What is the job of the write pointer in a compacting pattern?
choices: Jump to the last item first
blocks.why: The write pointer marks where the next kept value should be placed.

sections.title: Trace before changing code
sections.summary: Write the pair, comparison, and reason for each move.

blocks.title: Trace checklist
items: Write left **index**, right index, and the two **values**.
Stop when the **pointers** meet or cross.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Do not move a **pointer** just because the **loop** needs progress. Move it because the comparison proves that side can be discarded.

blocks.prompt: Why can `left < right` be the **loop** **condition** for pair checks?
choices: A pair needs two different positions
It checks the same item twice
blocks.why: When left meets right, there is no two-position pair left.

blocks.title: Check a palindrome inward
blocks.caption: Compare left and right characters before moving inward.

steps.what_changed: A palindrome check only needs to keep comparing mirrored positions.

steps.body: The middle e does not need a partner.
